results.authors: Mas JL, Derumeaux G, et al.
results.key_finding: PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy was superior to antiplatelet therapy alone in preventing recurrent stroke in patients aged 16-60 with cryptogenic stroke and PFO featuring atrial septal aneurysm or large shunt. results.authors: Saver JL, Carroll JD, et al.
results.key_finding: Transcatheter PFO closure with the Amplatzer PFO Occluder reduced recurrent ischemic stroke by 62% (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.18-0.79) versus medical therapy in patients with cryptogenic stroke and PFO over a median 5.9-year follow-up.
results.title: Long-Term Outcomes of Patent Foramen Ovale Closure (RESPECT Extended Follow-up)

results.authors: Kernan WN, Ovbiagele B, et al.
results.key_finding: For patients under 60 years with cryptogenic ischemic stroke attributed to paradoxical embolism through a PFO, closure may be considered particularly when high-risk PFO features are present (large shunt, atrial septal aneurysm). Extended cardiac monitoring is recommended in all cryptogenic stroke patients to exclude paroxysmal AF. Hypercoagulability workup including antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden, and prothrombin gene mutation is indicated in young cryptogenic stroke.
results.title: AHA/ASA Guidelines: Prevention of Stroke in Patients with Stroke and TIA

results.authors: Cramer SC, Rordorf G, et al.
results.key_finding: Lower extremity DVT is identified in 10-20% of cryptogenic stroke patients with PFO. Valsalva-provoking activities (heavy lifting, straining, coughing) and prolonged immobility create right-to-left shunting conditions that enable paradoxical embolism. The RoPE score estimates stroke-PFO causal probability; high RoPE scores (younger, no risk factors, cortical infarct) favor a causal relationship.
results.title: Paradoxical Embolism Through Patent Foramen Ovale: Role of DVT and Valsalva

key_clinical_evidence: Young patient with no conventional vascular risk factors presenting with isolated right homonymous hemianopia and mild right hemibody sensory loss: the left PCA territory is the anatomic explanation (left PCA supplies left primary visual cortex in the medial occipital lobe, causing contralateral right hemianopia)

The single greatest diagnostic error in young cryptogenic stroke is anchoring to 'cannot be a real stroke' — young age and absent risk factors do not exclude ischemic stroke; DWI confirmation is the critical step

The paradoxical-embolism pathway requires three concurrent elements: (1) a venous thrombus source (DVT, here DVT provoked by prolonged flight immobility + Factor V Leiden); (2) a right-to-left intracardiac shunt (PFO confirmed by TEE bubble study); (3) a precipitating Valsalva-type maneuver or pressure reversal to drive venous emboli into the arterial circulation

The markedly elevated D-dimer (1820 ng/mL) in a patient with left calf tenderness and 7.5-hour immobile flight is the venous-thrombosis signal — the source clue for paradoxical embolism, even before formal lower-extremity venous imaging is obtained

TEE with agitated-saline bubble study is the gold-standard test for PFO detection and shunt quantification — must be performed to confirm the paradoxical-embolism mechanism in any young cryptogenic stroke with suspected PFO

Factor V Leiden heterozygosity amplifies venous thrombosis risk 4-8 fold — the inherited thrombophilia provides biological plausibility for DVT formation during the flight and enhances the RoPE score-based case for a PFO-mediated mechanism
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

case_body_concerns: Lower-extremity venous imaging (e.g., compression ultrasound of bilateral leg veins for DVT) is the clinically critical test to confirm the venous source for paradoxical embolism, but this test is not available as a named tool in the 12-tool universe. The embedded clinical surrogates are: (1) markedly elevated D-dimer 1820 ng/mL in initial_tool_outputs.labs, and (2) left calf swelling and tenderness on neurological exam. The DVT diagnosis is therefore implied by these clinical data rather than confirmed by a dedicated tool output. Documented in vocab_gap.

clinical_pearls: LEFT PCA territory infarction causes RIGHT homonymous hemianopia (contralateral visual field loss) plus possible right thalamic sensory deficits — laterality is a non-negotiable internal consistency requirement
Paradoxical embolism via PFO is the most common mechanism of cryptogenic stroke in young adults under 45 — requires TEE bubble study to confirm and venous imaging to identify the DVT source

Prolonged immobility (long-haul flight, economy class) provokes DVT formation; Valsalva during disembarkation or straining provides the right-to-left pressure gradient to drive venous clot across a PFO
Factor V Leiden heterozygosity is the most prevalent inherited thrombophilia in Europeans and amplifies venous thrombosis risk 4-8 fold, potentiating paradoxical embolism in patients with a PFO

The RoPE score (Risk of Paradoxical Embolism) assigns high causal probability when the patient is young, has no vascular risk factors, and has a cortical infarct on imaging — all features present here

Alexia without agraphia (reading impaired, writing preserved) is a classic left PCA occlusion syndrome due to disconnection of the right visual cortex from left language areas via the splenium of the corpus callosum
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — 34-year-old man with no vascular risk factors presenting with isolated right homonymous hemianopia after a transatlantic flight. The puzzle: young age and visual symptoms anchor naive reasoning toward migraine with aura or functional disorder. The correct path requires DWI confirmation of a real left PCA infarct, then a systematic cryptogenic workup that uncovers: (1) elevated D-dimer and left calf tenderness suggesting DVT as the venous embolic source; (2) PFO with large right-to-left shunt on TEE bubble study; (3) heterozygous Factor V Leiden amplifying DVT risk. Together these establish paradoxical embolism as the mechanism. Requires synthesis across MRI, TEE bubble study, cardiac monitoring, and hypercoagulability data.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Young cryptogenic stroke with PFO/paradoxical embolism mechanism; requires synthesis of MRI-DWI confirmation, TEE bubble study, D-dimer/DVT evidence, hypercoagulability (Factor V Leiden), and prolonged rhythm monitoring; primary red herring is migraine-mimic anchor from young age and isolated visual symptoms.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case
vocab_gap: Lower-extremity venous compression ultrasound for DVT detection — required to confirm the venous thrombus source for paradoxical embolism, but no matching tool exists in the 12-tool set or order_advanced_imaging closed vocabulary. Clinical surrogates embedded in labs (D-dimer 1820 ng/mL) and exam (left calf tenderness/swelling). Proposed addition: order_advanced_imaging modality='venous_duplex_lower_extremity'.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marco Ferreira is a 34-year-old right-handed man with no significant past medical history who presents to the emergency department after acute onset of right-sided visual loss noticed upon waking this morning. He describes being unable to see anything to the right in both eyes. He also endorses mild numbness of the right face and right arm. His partner confirms he was neurologically normal at bedtime. He returned 48 hours ago from a transatlantic flight from Lisbon to Boston, approximately 7.5 hours in economy class with minimal mobility. He did not get up during the flight and slept for most of it. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes, cardiac disease, or prior neurological events. He has never had prior visual disturbances. He specifically denies any preceding scintillating scotoma, spreading visual aura, or throbbing headache that might suggest migraine aura. He has no prior history of migraines. His partner notes he had been rubbing his eyes and shaking his head on waking, wondering if it would pass. On arrival in the ED he reports the visual loss is persistent and unchanged. He denies chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, or leg swelling, though on directed questioning he admits to mild left calf aching since the flight, which he attributed to 'economy class syndrome.' He has no known family history of stroke. A paternal aunt had an unprovoked DVT at age 42. He takes no medications. He denies tobacco use and illicit drugs. Last known well is bedtime the prior evening, approximately 8 hours before presentation.
